# Abstract

Founded in 1894, Ocean Power Technologies (OPTT) is a martime-focused company with an emphasis on
finding solutions to the need for more efficient/productive infrastructure. Their
services span defense and security, oil and gas procurement, and off-shore wind markets.

OPTT went public on the NASDAQ on the 25th of April, 2007. Initially, the stock
exploded, with a closing price high of $3,652.00 on November 12th, 2007. Ever since,
the stock has been on the decline, falling under $5 per share in early 2019. Crossing
that $5 threshold means the stock is now classified as a penny stock. Ocean Power
Technologies hosts a market cap of $74.6 Million (at the time of writing), thus
designating the company as a micro-cap company.

Since approximately 2012, OPTT has suffered in many ways that have led to investor
dis-trust. The three main areas of concern are the high risk designation due to
high volatility, share dilution, and multi-million dollar operating losses. For
example, between 2012 and 2026, the number of shares (approximately) increased from
5 million to 180 million while total operating losses during that time exceeded
$300 Million.

That being said, OPTT is not entirely out of the market. On January 6th, 2026
OPTT announced they had been awarded a contract by the U.S. Department of Homeland
Security for the purpose of supplying the U.S. Coast Guard with their new
PowerBuoy systems. The contract was valued at $6.5 Million. This contract was not
only a lifeline for OPTT but marked the transition from a sustainability focused
private company into what is now essentially a revenue focused defense contractor.

In this project, I use statistical modelling and financial metrics to
analyse OPTT's performance and risk overtime. From there I aim to make inferences
about whether thus far the contract has begun to aid OPTT recover. I then test
my inferences using machine learning algorithms to predict future stock prices.

I will be using OLS regression models for performance analysis, using the log of
Volume as the dependent variable. I am using volume because in contrast to the
other metrics I can choose from, Volume is able to differentiate between direction
and attention in the market. Volume focuses on how many shares are bought or sold,
meaning it is a good measure of general activity surrounding the stock itself as
opposed to what the public think of the stock. I take the log of Volume due to
it being right-skewed with a median of 7,710 vs a mean of 1,974,392.

I will use an ordinal logistic regression model for risk analysis, using a "risk event"
severity level as the dependent variable. The risk event will be triggered when a significant
price drop or abnormal volume spike (in either direction) occurs, or both. The model is ordinal in nature,
with 3 "severity" tiers, defined as:

- **Level 1** -> No Risk Event: Price Drop < 3% and Volume Multiple < 1.25
- **Level 2** -> Moderate Risk Event: Price Drop between 3% - 7% (inclusive) or Volume
Multiple between 1.25 - 2 (inclusive) AND neither metric surpasses Level 3 thresholds.
- **Level 3** -> High Risk Event: Price Drop > 7% or Volume Multiple > 2

All predictors in the risk model are lagged by one day, so that the model only uses
information available before the day of the event.

I will then move into predictive modelling, using Random Forest, XGBoost, and LSTM Networks to
predict future performance.

For the LSTM Network, the adjusted closing price will be the
outcome variable. I am using adjusted closing over opening or closing price due
to the notion that an ML algorithm will look at fluctuations between day as catastrophic
economic events if the drop is significant enough from one day to another. It is
also of note that if that drop is caused by a volatility spike, the adjusted closing
price will catch it. Moreover, the adjusted closing price would back-trace historical
data which would prevent the model from falling for false inter-day price gaps.

For the Random Forest and XGBoost algorithms, it does not make sense to predict
price as a raw dollar metric due to the lack of trend-awareness that these
algorithms possess. Both algorithms function by breaking the data down into rectangular
cross sections based on real historic data. Thus, these models will never predict
a future dollar price that exceeds the upper and lower bounds of the data - a
reality that does not exist in the stock market. As a solution, I will predict
returns using the next-day log return as the outcome variable (the log of tomorrow's
adjusted closing price divided by today's, in percent). Log returns are used because they are
symmetric and far less sensitive to extreme days than simple percent changes

To conclude, I will compare the effectiveness of the 3 ML models using error scores
to determine which stand-alone algorithm performed best.

Why does any of this matter? Firstly, I enjoy machine learning and investing,
so this was a natural project for me to take on. Secondly, it is an interesting
question to ask - can traditional ML handle the noise of penny stocks? Currently,
analysts rely on hybrid algorithms that incorporate classification models *and*
sentiment analysis. In most cases, LSTMs tend to confuse the noise of unexpected
price spikes (that are overly common in penny stocks) for true trends, and I want to
see the comparison myself.

# The Data

In order to take on this project, I utilise a variety of methods to procure data.
The main pathway is the `tidyquant` package from which I am able to download
historic data about the desired ticker. `tidyquant` primarily leans on Yahoo
Finance for key metrics, but also pulls from several other databases such as
the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED).

I also make queries to NewsAPI and Finnhub, two APIs that allow me to scrape for
media related to my chosen ticker in order to perform sentiment analysis in
conjunction with the machine learning models. Unfortunately, there is limited
results for Ocean Power Technologies and as such I do not continue down this path.

Using `tidyquant`, I retrieve data from April 25th, 2007 (IPO) until June 21st,
2026 which is the date of writing, although the data becomes usable after row 34
due to the staggered system in which some calculated metrics such as MACD work.
That being said, the complete dataset boasts 4,819 observations across 17
variables (22 when including ticker name, year, month, month name, and day).

Of these 17 variables, some notable measures include:

- **`open_price`**: Stock price at open on a given trading day
- **`close_price`**: Stock price at close on a given trading day
- **`Volume`**: Number of shares traded (bought or sold) during a given trading day
- **`true_range`**: Total price volatility by finding the greatest distance between current high, current low and previous closing price, as a percent of the closing price
- **`ATR`**: Moving average of true range over a 14-day period (also a percent of the closing price)
- **`rsi`**: Relative Strength Index: Measures magnitude and speed of price fluctuations on a scale of 0-100 (momentum indicator)
- **`macd_hist`**: Measures if the stock's momentum is speeding up or slowing down
- **`obv`**: On-Balance Volume: Relationship metric between volume and price used to spot divergences

To illustrate the structured dataset, rows 34–39 are displayed below. Because
several indicators rely on rolling or exponential moving-average calculations of
varying lengths (e.g., a 14-day window for ATR and RSI, and a 26-day EMA -
Exponential Moving Average - for the MACD trendline, followed by a further 9-day
EMA for the MACD signal line), the initial rows of the dataset default to NA
values until each indicator has accumulated sufficient historical data to produce
a valid output. The MACD signal line, in particular, does not return numeric
values until row 34, as it requires the MACD line itself to first be calculated.
Rows 34–39 are therefore displayed to ensure all indicators, including MACD and
its derived histogram, are represented with complete, numeric, and non-NA values.

In short, the following table represents values from June 12th, 2007 - June 19th,
2007. June 16 and June 17 are omitted as they fall on a Saturday and Sunday which
are non-trading days, meaning no data can be collected on those days.

Before computing any indicators, I check the price history for impossible one-day jumps.
Yahoo Finance adjusts old prices for stock splits, but a split that is only partly adjusted, or a bad
price record, shows up as a one-day move of several hundred percent that would dominate every error
score downstream. The check below lists every day where the adjusted close more than triples or falls
by more than two thirds, and sorts each one into one of three kinds, using that day's trading volume
to tell them apart. A real split changes the price and the number of shares traded in opposite
directions, so price times volume stays about the same. A **split** persists, is within 15% of a
standard split ratio, and has that opposite-moving volume: prices before that day are rescaled to the
post-split basis and Volume is rescaled the opposite way. A **spike** is followed within five trading
days by a jump back to about the original level, which makes it a one-off bad record, and the affected
days are removed. Anything else, such as a one-day jump that comes with a huge surge in volume, is a
**real move** and is kept. Finally, open, high and low are scaled by the adjusted-to-close ratio so that
every price in the dataset, and every indicator built from it, sits on the same adjusted basis.

```{r}
#| output: true

#price integrity check: flag days where the adjusted close more than triples (+200%)
#or falls by more than two thirds (-67%)
price_check <- optt |>
  mutate(row = row_number(), daily_ratio = adjusted / lag(adjusted))

extreme_days <- price_check |>
  filter(daily_ratio > 3 | daily_ratio < 1 / 3) |>
  select(row, date, close, adjusted, daily_ratio)

#standard split ratios (reverse or forward). A flagged jump within 15% of one of these
#is treated as an unadjusted split
split_ratios <- c(2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 100)

#a one-off bad record shows up as a big jump followed within 5 trading days by a jump back to about
#the original level (the two jumps roughly cancel). That is a bad record, not a split
extreme_days$spike_end_row <- NA_integer_
for (k in seq_len(nrow(extreme_days))) {
  later <- which(extreme_days$row > extreme_days$row[k] &
                   extreme_days$row <= extreme_days$row[k] + 5 &
                   sign(log(extreme_days$daily_ratio)) == -sign(log(extreme_days$daily_ratio[k])) &
                   abs(log(extreme_days$daily_ratio[k] * extreme_days$daily_ratio)) < log(2))
  if (length(later) > 0) extreme_days$spike_end_row[k] <- extreme_days$row[later[1]]
}

#a real split moves price and share volume in opposite directions, so (price ratio) x (volume ratio)
#stays about 1. Volume ratio = the jump day's volume relative to the median of the 5 days before it
extreme_days$volume_ratio <- sapply(extreme_days$row, function(r) {
  prior <- optt$volume[max(1, r - 5):(r - 1)]
  optt$volume[r] / max(median(prior), 1)
})

extreme_days <- extreme_days |>
  mutate(
    is_spike = !is.na(spike_end_row),
    is_spike_end = row %in% spike_end_row, #the jump back at the end of a spike
    jump_size = if_else(daily_ratio > 1, daily_ratio, 1 / daily_ratio),
    nearest_split = map_dbl(jump_size, function(j) split_ratios[which.min(abs(j / split_ratios - 1))]),
    dollar_ratio = daily_ratio * volume_ratio,
    volume_confirms_split = dollar_ratio > 0.2 & dollar_ratio < 5,
    is_split = !is_spike & !is_spike_end & abs(jump_size / nearest_split - 1) < 0.15 & volume_confirms_split,
    #prices BEFORE the jump are rescaled to the post-jump basis:
    #a reverse split (price jumps up) multiplies them, a forward split divides them
    rescale_factor = if_else(daily_ratio > 1, nearest_split, 1 / nearest_split),
    treatment = case_when(
      is_spike | is_spike_end ~ "bad record (spike), removed",
      is_split ~ "unadjusted split, rescaled",
      TRUE ~ "real move, kept"
    )
  )

extreme_days |>
  select(date, adjusted, daily_ratio, volume_ratio, dollar_ratio, treatment) |>
  kable(digits = 3) |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 10)
```

```{r}
#first remove the bad records: the rows from the start of each spike up to (not including)
#the day of the jump back
spike_rows <- unlist(lapply(which(extreme_days$is_spike), function(k) {
  extreme_days$row[k]:(extreme_days$spike_end_row[k] - 1)
}))
if (length(spike_rows) > 0) optt <- optt[-spike_rows, ]

#then rescale prices (and Volume the opposite way) before each unadjusted split
adj_factor <- rep(1, nrow(optt))
for (i in which(extreme_days$is_split)) {
  before_jump <- optt$date < extreme_days$date[i]
  adj_factor[before_jump] <- adj_factor[before_jump] * extreme_days$rescale_factor[i]
}

optt <- optt |>
  mutate(
    across(c(open, high, low, close, adjusted), ~ .x * adj_factor),
    volume = volume / adj_factor,
    #put open/high/low/close on the adjusted basis too, so every indicator is built
    #from one consistent price series
    price_basis = adjusted / close,
    open = open * price_basis,
    high = high * price_basis,
    low = low * price_basis,
    close = adjusted
  ) |>
  select(-price_basis)
```

```{r}
#| output: true

#days classed as real moves are kept (a one-day jump with a matching surge in volume is a genuine event).
#after the cleaning, the only days still flagged should be those real moves
real_moves <- extreme_days$date[extreme_days$treatment == "real move, kept"]
remaining <- optt |>
  mutate(daily_ratio = adjusted / lag(adjusted)) |>
  filter(daily_ratio > 3 | daily_ratio < 1 / 3)
unexpected <- remaining |> filter(!(date %in% real_moves))
if (nrow(unexpected) > 0) warning("Unexpected extreme price jumps remain after cleaning: inspect `unexpected`")

cat("Days flagged:", nrow(extreme_days),
    "| splits rescaled:", sum(extreme_days$treatment == "unadjusted split, rescaled"),
    "| spike rows removed:", length(spike_rows),
    "| real moves kept:", length(real_moves),
    "| unexpected jumps remaining:", nrow(unexpected), "\n")
```

```{r}
#tidy datatable

#rename variables to be more
optt_tidy <- optt |>
  rename(open_price = open,
         high_price = high,
         low_price = low,
         close_price = close,
         Volume = volume,
         Adjusted = adjusted) |>

#break date into day, month, year columns
  separate(date, into = c("Year", "Month", "Day"), sep = "-", convert = TRUE) |>

#add month name column
  mutate(month_name = month.name[Month]) |>

#place month name column after month number
  relocate(month_name, .after = Month) |>

#create new variables
  mutate(
    #intra-day volatility
    idv = (high_price-low_price),
    #previous close price
    prev_close = lag(close_price),
    #absolute maximum upward movement
    max_up = (abs(high_price - prev_close)),
    #absolute maximum downward movement
    max_down = (abs(low_price - prev_close)),
    #true range, as a percent of that day's closing price:
    #use pmax (parallel max) to take max for each day --> eliminates need for if/else + max()
    #divide by close_price so volatility is comparable across the full price history ($3,652 to under $1)
    true_range = 100 * pmax(idv, max_up, max_down, na.rm = TRUE) / close_price,
    #average true range (percent):
    #use rollmean (zoo package) to look at a sliding window
    ATR = rollmean(true_range, k = 14, fill = NA, align = "right"),
    #RSI - Relative Strength Index - measures momentum (magnitude and speed of price fluctuations, 0-100)
    rsi = RSI(close_price, n = 14),
    #MACD - Moving Average Convergence Divergence
    #helps identify whether stock has sustained movement or just noisy movement.
    macd_trendline = MACD(close_price, nFast = 12, nSlow = 26, nSig = 9)[, "macd"],
    macd_signal = MACD(close_price, nFast = 12, nSlow = 26, nSig = 9)[, "signal"],
    #the distance between macd trend and signal is macd histogram
    #acts as a measure of how strong the bullish or bearish momentum is
    macd_hist = (macd_trendline - macd_signal),
    #On Balance Volume (OBV):
    #essentially functions as a validity check of the price trend.
    obv = OBV(close_price, Volume)
  )
```

## MACD Explained

MACD is the Moving Average Convergence Divergence, essentially a
tool used to determine buy/sell signals, price trends, and momentum. There are 3
main parts to MACD: the trendline, the signal line, and the histogram.

The MACD trendline is the main part of this indicator. It is calculated as the
percentage difference between a 12-period EMA and a 26-period EMA (the default in
`TTR::MACD`), meaning all three MACD values are already scaled by price. The 26-period EMA is the
longer-term trend and the 12-period EMA is the shorter-term momentum. EMA stands
for Exponential Moving Average and is a metric that smooths out the price data
to gauge a better view of the direction and momentum of trends. It is used over
standard moving averages because it puts higher emphasis on later data points,
which matter most in the stock market. Due to the volatility of the OPTT stock,
I elect to use 12 and 26 period EMAs as opposed to 50 and 200 period EMAs which
might be more favourable to longer term analysis or more stable stocks.

The MACD signal line is a 9-period moving average of the MACD trendline. In
other words, it acts as a "slower" baseline metric for the momentum of the stock
which can then be compared to the "faster" trendline.

That relationship is expressed by the MACD histogram. It is a metric that helps
investors determine it is a bullish vs bearish market, which in turn aids in
determining whether or not to buy or sell the stock. I calculate this value by
subtracting the MACD signal from the MACD trendline value for any given
observation, represented as `macd_hist` in the table above (in percentage points).

Below are the values of the MACD histogram displayed as a histogram:

```{r}
#| output: true

#macd histogram
hist <- ggplot(optt_tidy, aes(x=macd_hist)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", colour = "navy", bins = 100) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", size = 0.75, colour = "red") +
  labs(title = "MACD Histogram Distribution",
       subtitle = "Ticker: OPTT",
       x = "MACD Histogram Value (percentage points)",
       y = "Frequency") +
  theme_classic()


hist
```

Looking at the pictured histogram, we see that the data is (for the most part),
normally distributed around 0 with a slight right-skew. This tells me that on
average, across all time, momentum is neutral, meaning no real sustained bullish
nor bearish trends. The extended tail that causes the right-skew is most likely
a result of the initial bullish trend when the company first became public on the
NASDAQ. This would explain why we don't see a tail of equal length on the left:
the decline was slower, across a longer period of time, meaning the fluctuations
during the decline will mitigate the effect of that sustained decline. On a
similar stream, we would expect the MACD histogram of a higher valued, more stable
stock to have a tighter distribution. For example, an S&P500 tracker like VOO
could be expected to have a tighter distribution with a slight right-shift (not skew)
due to it's sustained upward trend without the extreme volatility witnessed in
OPTT.

# Sentiment Analysis

```{r}
#Sentiment news data is cached in Sentiment_Cache.csv.
#The APIs are only queried if the cache file does not exist.
cache_file <- "Sentiment_Cache.csv"

if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
  scraped <- read_csv(cache_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
} else {
  if (finnhub_key == "" || news_api_key == "") {
    stop("FINNHUB_API_KEY / NEWS_API_KEY not set (restore .Renviron and restart R), ",
         "and no Sentiment_Cache.csv exists.")
  }

  #finnhub Sentiment News Scoring
  finnhub_url <- paste0(
    "https://finnhub.io/api/v1/company-news?symbol=OPTT&from=2026-10-12&to=2026-11-10&token=", finnhub_key)

  #process data using httr and jsonlite
  finnhub_raw_data <- GET(finnhub_url)
  stop_for_status(finnhub_raw_data)  #errors clearly on a bad key / rate limit
  finnhub_parsed <- fromJSON(content(finnhub_raw_data, "text"))
  if (!is.data.frame(finnhub_parsed)) {
    #Finnhub returns [] when no articles match, which parses to an empty list
    finnhub_parsed <- tibble(datetime = numeric(), headline = character(),
                             source = character(), url = character())
  }

  #clean parsed data into a usable format
  finnhub_tidy <- finnhub_parsed |>
    mutate(
      Date = as_date(as_datetime(datetime)),
      Text = headline
    ) |>
    rename(Source = source) |>
    select(Date, Text, Source, url)

  # News API Sentiment Scoring
  news_api_result <- get_everything(
    query = '"Ocean Power Technologies" OR "OPTT stock" OR "NASDAQ:OPTT"',
    from = "2026-10-12",
    to = "2026-11-10",
    api_key = news_api_key
  )

  #clean news api data
  news_df <- news_api_result$results_df
  if (is.null(news_df) || nrow(news_df) == 0) {
    #no articles matched: use an empty table with the expected columns
    news_df <- tibble(published_at = as.POSIXct(character()), title = character(),
                      name = character(), url = character())
  }
  news_tidy <- news_df |>
    mutate(
      #change column names to match finnhub to make joining easier
      Date = as_date(published_at),
      Text = title
    ) |>
    rename(Source = name) |>
    select(Date, Text, Source, url)

  #combine scraped data and save to cache
  scraped <- full_join(finnhub_tidy, news_tidy, by = c("Date", "Text", "Source", "url"))
  write_csv(scraped, cache_file)
}
```

After querying both NewsAPI and Finnhub, across many trial runs between June and August 2026, on average 6 articles were returned,
primarily originating from sources of high bias.
Due to concerns of limited data and subsequent biases, I will not be using sentiment analysis
scores within my models. The table below shows the date and source of each relevant article.

These articles are not sufficient in terms of volume, however if used, another
bias concern would arise: on average 43.75% of represented information would stem from the same
source - GlobeNewswire. GlobeNewswire is not an independent journalism company, rather
the company is paid by other companies (like Ocean Power Technologies) to publish
and distribute press releases. In other words, the publications represented in
this scenario were written by Ocean Power Technologies themselves.

Instead of sentiment data, the following analysis will focus on price-derived
technical indicators alongside trading volume. These variables are derived directly
from empirical trading data, avoiding the sample-size and bias concerns associated
with the limited sentiment data.

In order to maintain structural robustness via alternative data streams, the analysis
will pivot to integrate macroeconomic corporate health metrics, specifically
outstanding share dilution and top-line revenue recovery.

# Alternate Data Procurement

To supplement the market data, I require fundamental financial metrics to accurately
gauge the internal health of the company. Specifically, I focus on Outstanding Shares,
Net Loss, and Revenue. The original CSVs I had scraped from SEC filings using Google's
NotebookLM (`order_backlog.csv` and `OPTT_Data.csv`) were lost, and were not recoverable
from local backups. Rather than re-scrape SEC filings by hand, I instead source the same
underlying figures directly from OPTT's filed 10-Ks through the SEC's XBRL data service
(see References). An earlier version of this dataset used a third-party aggregator, but
checking it against the filings showed that many of its figures did not match the 10-Ks,
so it was replaced. This lets me rebuild the alternate dataset transparently and reproducibly.

While I was rebuilding this dataset, I also reconsidered the Backlog-Sales Ratio I had
originally planned to use. As noted earlier, order backlog was not reported by OPTT
between 2015 and 2020 (a gap I had been forced to impute with \$0), which biases any
series built from it. **Revenue** does not have this problem - it is disclosed every
fiscal year without exception - and it more directly tests the question I actually
care about: whether the January 2026 U.S. Coast Guard/DHS contract is translating into
top-line recovery. I therefore drop the Backlog-Sales Ratio entirely in favour of Revenue.

Similarly, the figures I use report **Net Loss** (the income-statement bottom line)
rather than Operating Loss specifically. I use Net Loss instead of Operating Loss. This is not simply a
data-availability compromise: OPTT's bottom line is also driven by large non-cash
fair-value adjustments on warrants and other derivative liabilities issued as part of
its dilutive financings, so Net Loss captures more of the dilution-and-risk story the
Abstract describes than Operating Loss would.

Outstanding Shares are only used from fiscal 2019 onward - before that, OPTT's reverse
stock splits mean the cover-page share counts are not on a comparable basis, and I leave
those years as `NA` rather than fabricate a number. Revenue and Net Loss are available back to fiscal 2012, which
conveniently lines up with the Abstract's own framing of 2012 as when OPTT's dilution
and loss problems began, so I restrict the alternate dataset to fiscal years 2012-2026.
OPTT's fiscal year runs May-April, so "fiscal 2012" covers May 2011 - April 2012, and
so on.

```{r}
#Annual fundamentals for OPTT, fiscal years 2012-2026 (FY ends April 30).
#Sourced directly from OPTT's 10-K filings through the SEC XBRL API
#(data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyconcept/CIK0001378140), retrieved 2026-11-25 - see References.
#revenue and net_loss: the value reported for that fiscal year in the most recent 10-K that
#  reports it (FY2019 revenue is the later 600,000; it was first reported as 632,000).
#shares_outstanding: the cover-page share count in that fiscal year's 10-K (as of the filing date).
#  Only FY2019 onward is used: earlier counts are not on a comparable basis because of OPTT's
#  reverse stock splits, so earlier years are left NA rather than guessed at.
#filed_date: the date that fiscal year's 10-K was filed, i.e. when the figures became public.

alt_data_annual <- tibble(
  fiscal_year = 2012:2026,
  revenue = c(5738506, 3616129, 1498892, 4105424, 704820, 843000, 511000,
              600000, 1682000, 1206000, 1759000, 2732000, 5525000, 5861000, 3737000),
  net_loss = c(-15140502, -14681837, -10969192, -13114552, -13129000, -9486000, -10157000,
               -12246000, -10352000, -14760000, -18874000, -26326000, -27483000, -24466000, -48915000),
  shares_outstanding = c(rep(NA_real_, 7),
                         5771747, 17120565, 52458011, 55881861, 58730917, 92708981, 177542775, 270138823),
  filed_date = as.Date(c("2012-07-13", "2013-07-12", "2014-07-29", "2015-07-06", "2016-07-15",
                         "2017-07-14", "2018-07-17", "2019-07-22", "2020-06-29", "2021-07-19",
                         "2022-07-13", "2023-07-28", "2024-07-25", "2025-07-24", "2026-08-19"))
)

head(alt_data_annual)
```

Because these fundamentals are reported annually rather than quarterly (as I had
originally assumed) and the main dataset is daily rather than monthly, disaggregating
straight to monthly - as I had originally planned - would not have actually solved
the alignment problem at all. Linear interpolation is still ruled out for the same
look-ahead reason as before, and plain LOCF still introduces the same volatility
attenuation and false-stability bias described earlier, now stretched across an
entire year instead of a quarter, which makes it worse, not better.

I still favour the temporal disaggregation approach over these alternatives, but I
disaggregate the annual figures down to **fiscal quarters** rather than months, since
a 4x annual-to-quarterly ratio is well supported by the `tempdisagg` package and
quarterly is the natural reporting cadence for a company of this size, even though I
can only source annual totals. Each trading day then simply inherits the modelled
value for the fiscal quarter it falls in. This is not the naive LOCF I ruled out above:
the quarterly series itself already carries model-implied sub-annual variation from
the disaggregation step, tracked against a correlated daily indicator; only the last
step (quarter -> individual trading day) is a step function, which mirrors how the
market actually receives this information - a filed number that is valid until the
next filing, not a value that drifts continuously day to day.

I also distinguish between the two kinds of fundamentals I have: Revenue and Net Loss
are *flow* variables (they accumulate over the year), so the quarterly figures must
sum back to the annual total. Outstanding Shares is a *stock* variable (a point-in-time
count), so the quarterly figure must instead match the annual figure at fiscal
year-end. Applying a "sum" conversion to Outstanding Shares, or a "last" conversion to
Revenue, would silently misrepresent the data, so `tempdisagg`'s `conversion` argument
is set differently for each.

As before, I use the Litterman method, i.e. the Random Walk-Markov extension of
Chow-Lin, with trading Volume as the correlated higher-frequency indicator, since it
lets the interpolated path drift rather than snapping back to the mean every quarter -
appropriate given OPTT's persistent negative drift. If a given series' fit is poor
(low R^2 / implausible autocorrelation parameter), Denton-Cholette is the fallback,
since it guarantees a smooth, well-behaved path even without a strong indicator
relationship - I did not need to fall back to it for any of the three series below,
but flag it as the next step if new fundamentals are added later. A GARCH-based
enhancement to model time-varying volatility in the disaggregated residuals, as I had
originally hoped for, is not something `tempdisagg` supports out of the box, so it
remains a possible future refinement rather than something implemented here.

The two chunks below are kept as a record of this abandoned approach and are no longer
evaluated (`eval: false`), because the quarterly series is not used by any model and the
annual figures it was built from have since been replaced with figures taken directly from
OPTT's 10-Ks.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#build the fiscal calendar on the main (daily) data, without altering optt_tidy itself
optt_fiscal_calendar <- optt_tidy |>
  select(Year, Month, Volume) |>
  mutate(
    #OPTT's fiscal year runs May - April, so fiscal year = calendar year + 1 for May-Dec
    fiscal_year = if_else(Month >= 5, Year + 1, Year),
    #fiscal month index: May = 1 ... April = 12
    fiscal_month = ((Month - 5) %% 12) + 1,
    fiscal_quarter = ceiling(fiscal_month / 3)
  )
#NOTE: kept at full length (one row per optt_tidy row, 2007-2026) so it can be
#bound back onto optt_tidy below; the fiscal_year restriction to 2012-2026 (the
#span alt_data_annual covers) is applied only when building the indicator next.

#daily Volume aggregated up to (fiscal year, fiscal quarter) - the correlated
#higher-frequency indicator used by the Litterman/Chow-Lin regression below
optt_quarterly_indicator <- optt_fiscal_calendar |>
  filter(fiscal_year >= 2012, fiscal_year <= 2026) |>
  group_by(fiscal_year, fiscal_quarter) |>
  summarise(mean_volume = mean(Volume, na.rm = TRUE),
            trading_days = n(),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(fiscal_year, fiscal_quarter)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tempdisagg)

#low-frequency (annual) series, one point per fiscal year
revenue_annual  <- ts(alt_data_annual$revenue,  start = 2012, frequency = 1)
loss_annual     <- ts(alt_data_annual$net_loss, start = 2012, frequency = 1)
#shares outstanding is only usable from FY2019 onward
shares_annual   <- ts(alt_data_annual$shares_outstanding[alt_data_annual$fiscal_year >= 2019],
                       start = 2019, frequency = 1)

#correlated high-frequency (fiscal-quarterly) indicator, same span as each annual series
volume_quarterly_full  <- ts(optt_quarterly_indicator$mean_volume, start = c(2012, 1), frequency = 4)
volume_quarterly_2019  <- ts(optt_quarterly_indicator$mean_volume[optt_quarterly_indicator$fiscal_year >= 2019],
                              start = c(2019, 1), frequency = 4)

#flow variables (revenue, net loss): quarterly figures must SUM to the annual total
model_revenue <- td(revenue_annual ~ volume_quarterly_full,
                     method = "litterman-maxlog", conversion = "sum")
model_loss    <- td(loss_annual ~ volume_quarterly_full,
                     method = "litterman-maxlog", conversion = "sum")
#stock variable (shares outstanding): quarterly figures must match the annual LAST value
model_shares  <- td(shares_annual ~ volume_quarterly_2019,
                     method = "litterman-maxlog", conversion = "last")

#shares_outstanding_q only has values for fiscal 2019 onward (model_shares' own span),
#so it is built and joined separately rather than assigned inside one mutate() -
#the vectors involved are different lengths and shouldn't be forced to line up positionally.
shares_quarterly <- optt_quarterly_indicator |>
  filter(fiscal_year >= 2019) |>
  mutate(shares_outstanding_q = as.numeric(predict(model_shares))) |>
  select(fiscal_year, fiscal_quarter, shares_outstanding_q)

alt_data_quarterly <- optt_quarterly_indicator |>
  mutate(
    revenue_q = as.numeric(predict(model_revenue)),
    net_loss_q = as.numeric(predict(model_loss))
  ) |>
  left_join(shares_quarterly, by = c("fiscal_year", "fiscal_quarter")) |>
  select(fiscal_year, fiscal_quarter, revenue_q, net_loss_q, shares_outstanding_q)
```

I still favour temporal disaggregation in principle, so the quarterly series above stays
in the project, but I elect not to use it in the modelling dataframe. This is because it
caused two problems. The first is that Volume is the outcome variable in my OLS model,
meaning Revenue and Net Loss built using Volume would partly contain the very outcome I
am trying to explain. The second is that spreading a fiscal year's figures across that
whole year gives the model information that did not exist yet: these numbers are not
public until OPTT files its 10-K, which happens a couple of months after the April 30th
year-end.

As a solution, each trading day instead takes the most recent annual figures that had
actually been filed by that date. Each fiscal year's figures become available on the date its 10-K
was actually filed with the SEC (between late June and late August, see References). This is a
step function, which mirrors how the market actually receives this information - a filed
number that is valid until the next filing. That being said, trading days before July 13th,
2012 have no fundamentals, and the FY2026 figures only become available on August 19th, 2026,
after the last day of data (June 21st, 2026), meaning the most recent trading days carry
the FY2025 figures.

```{r}
#date each fiscal year's figures become public (the date its 10-K was filed)
alt_data_annual <- alt_data_annual |>
  mutate(available_from = filed_date)
```

With the availability dates attached, I join the figures onto every trading day, then drop
the leading rows that are unusable regardless (rows 1-33, where MACD/MACD-signal have
not yet accumulated enough history), to produce the final dataframe used for modelling.

```{r}
#join main (daily) data with the annual alt data as of each trading day (most recent
#figures already filed), then tidy for model use
optt_model <- optt_tidy |>
  mutate(Date = make_date(Year, Month, Day)) |>
  left_join(alt_data_annual, by = join_by(closest(Date >= available_from)))

optt_model_tidy <- optt_model |>
  #row 33 is the last row with NA MACD/MACD-signal values (see "The Data" above)
  slice(34:n())

head(optt_model_tidy)
summary(optt_model_tidy)

```

```{r}
#keep only the data after June 2016: Yahoo's trading volume before then is on a much smaller scale
#(about 100-1,000 shares a day to May 2016, then tens of thousands to millions), which would distort
#every volume-based variable. The 1 June 2016 price jump itself is real and is not the reason for the cut.
optt_model_tidy <- optt_model_tidy |>
  filter(Date >= as.Date("2016-07-01"))
```
# Problem - shares outstanding has MANY n/a values --> can't really be used in modelling as is. 

# Historical Analysis:

# Ordinary Linear Squares Regression Model

```{r}
#obv is left out (it is built from Volume, the outcome) and so is macd_signal (macd_hist is already
#macd - signal). Price, shares and net loss are trending levels, so price and shares are logged and
#net loss is put in millions. Zero-volume days are dropped as log(0) is undefined.
#shares_outstanding and net_loss only exist from the FY2019 10-K onward, so lm() would silently drop every
#earlier day. The sample is built explicitly here so its size and dates can be reported.
ols_data <- optt_model_tidy |>
  filter(Volume > 0, !is.na(shares_outstanding), !is.na(net_loss))

ols_volume <- lm(log(Volume) ~ rsi + macd_hist + log(shares_outstanding) + I(net_loss / 1e6) + log(Adjusted),
          data = ols_data)
summary(ols_volume)

#daily data are autocorrelated, so the ordinary standard errors above are too small.
#Newey-West (HAC) standard errors (20 lags, about one trading month) are used for inference instead.
ols_volume_hac <- coeftest(ols_volume, vcov. = NeweyWest(ols_volume, lag = 20, prewhite = FALSE))
ols_volume_hac

#the sample actually used
cat("OLS (log Volume) sample:", nobs(ols_volume), "days,",
    format(min(ols_data$Date)), "to", format(max(ols_data$Date)), "\n")
```

```{r}
plot(ols_volume)
```


```{r}

#same changes as above; obv is cumulative (a trending level) so it is left out here too, and Volume is logged
#the model is named ols_atr because it explains the (log) ATR, a volatility measure, not price
ols_data_atr <- optt_model_tidy |>
  filter(Volume > 0, ATR > 0, !is.na(shares_outstanding), !is.na(net_loss))

ols_atr <- lm(log(ATR) ~ rsi + macd_hist + log(shares_outstanding) + I(net_loss / 1e6) + log(Volume) + log(Adjusted),
          data = ols_data_atr)
summary(ols_atr)

#ATR is a 14-day rolling mean, so neighbouring days share most of their data: HAC standard errors again
ols_atr_hac <- coeftest(ols_atr, vcov. = NeweyWest(ols_atr, lag = 20, prewhite = FALSE))
ols_atr_hac

cat("OLS (log ATR) sample:", nobs(ols_atr), "days,",
    format(min(ols_data_atr$Date)), "to", format(max(ols_data_atr$Date)), "\n")
```

```{r}
#check residuals
plot(ols_atr)
```

The coefficients in both regressions describe associations between same-day values, not
predictions or causal effects. Both models are fitted only on the days from the FY2019 10-K
onward, since that is when share counts become usable, and inference uses Newey-West standard
errors because daily observations are autocorrelated. Net loss and shares outstanding change only
once a year, so within this sample they largely act as a marker of the time period; they are
included as controls and I do not interpret their coefficients as effects.

# Risk Modelling:

# Ordinal Logistic Regression Model

```{r}
#ordinal logistic regression using MASS::polr (called with MASS:: so it does not mask dplyr::select)

#define the levels and metrics:
#The risk event will be triggered when a significant price drop or abnormal volume spike (in either direction)
#occurs, or both. Volume Multiple has no direction, so the volume trigger flags unusually high activity on
#any day: this is an abnormal-activity risk indicator, not a pure sell-side measure.

#- **Level 1** -> No Risk Event: Price Drop < 3% and Volume Multiple < 1.25
# **Level 2** -> Moderate Risk Event: Price Drop between 3% - 7% (inclusive) or Volume
#Multiple between 1.25 - 2 (inclusive) AND neither metric surpasses Level 3 thresholds.
#- **Level 3** -> High Risk Event: Price Drop > 7% or Volume Multiple > 2

#volume multiple = Current Volume ÷ Average Volume (use 15 day moving avg)
#the average uses the 15 days BEFORE the current day, so a spike cannot dilute its own average

#the data are built in a function so the cut-offs can be varied in the sensitivity check below.
#the defaults are the thresholds above
build_risk_data <- function(drop_mod = 0.03, drop_high = 0.07, vol_mod = 1.25, vol_high = 2) {
  optt_model_tidy |>
    mutate(
      #price drop (as a fraction) from the previous day's adjusted close, gains count as 0
      price_drop = pmax(0, -(Adjusted / lag(Adjusted) - 1)),
      vol_avg15 = lag(rollmean(Volume, k = 15, fill = NA, align = "right")),
      vol_multiple = Volume / vol_avg15,
      risk_level = case_when(
        is.na(price_drop) | !is.finite(vol_multiple) ~ NA_character_,
        price_drop > drop_high | vol_multiple > vol_high ~ "Level 3",
        price_drop >= drop_mod | vol_multiple >= vol_mod ~ "Level 2",
        TRUE ~ "Level 1"
      ),
      risk_level = factor(risk_level, levels = c("Level 1", "Level 2", "Level 3"), ordered = TRUE),
      log_vol_multiple = log(vol_multiple),
      #predictors are lagged one day so the model only uses information available before the event day
      rsi_lag = lag(rsi),
      macd_hist_lag = lag(macd_hist),
      ATR_lag = lag(ATR),
      price_drop_lag = lag(price_drop),
      log_vol_multiple_lag = lag(log_vol_multiple)
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(risk_level),
           is.finite(rsi_lag), is.finite(macd_hist_lag), is.finite(ATR_lag),
           is.finite(price_drop_lag), is.finite(log_vol_multiple_lag))
}

risk_data <- build_risk_data()

risk_formula <- risk_level ~ rsi_lag + macd_hist_lag + ATR_lag + price_drop_lag + log_vol_multiple_lag
risk_model <- MASS::polr(risk_formula, data = risk_data, Hess = TRUE)
summary(risk_model)

#polr does not report p-values, so calculate them from the t values
#(these assume independent days, so they are too optimistic: see the block bootstrap below)
risk_coefs <- coef(summary(risk_model))
cbind(risk_coefs, p_value = 2 * pnorm(abs(risk_coefs[, "t value"]), lower.tail = FALSE))

#odds ratios
exp(coef(risk_model))
```

Risk events cluster in time, so the standard errors that `polr` reports (which treat every day as
independent) are too small. The block bootstrap below resamples 20-day blocks of consecutive days, which
keeps that clustering, and the Brant test checks the proportional odds assumption that an ordinal
logistic model relies on.

```{r}
#| output: true

#moving-block bootstrap standard errors: resample 20-day blocks of consecutive days
set.seed(11142026)
n_risk <- nrow(risk_data)
block_len <- 20
n_boot <- 200
boot_coefs <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_boot, ncol = length(coef(risk_model)))

for (b in seq_len(n_boot)) {
  starts <- sample(seq_len(n_risk - block_len + 1), size = ceiling(n_risk / block_len), replace = TRUE)
  idx <- unlist(lapply(starts, function(s) s:(s + block_len - 1)))[seq_len(n_risk)]
  fit_b <- tryCatch(MASS::polr(risk_formula, data = risk_data[idx, ], Hess = FALSE),
                    error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(fit_b)) boot_coefs[b, ] <- coef(fit_b)
}

boot_se <- apply(boot_coefs, 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE)
risk_boot_table <- tibble(
  term = names(coef(risk_model)),
  estimate = as.numeric(coef(risk_model)),
  boot_se = boot_se,
  z = estimate / boot_se,
  p_value = 2 * pnorm(abs(z), lower.tail = FALSE)
)

risk_boot_table |>
  kable(digits = 4) |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 10)

#Brant test of the proportional odds assumption (small p-values mean the assumption is doubtful)
if (requireNamespace("brant", quietly = TRUE)) {
  brant::brant(risk_model)
} else {
  cat("Install the 'brant' package to run the proportional odds test.\n")
}
```

The cut-offs (3% and 7% price drops, 1.25x and 2x volume) are conventions I chose, not estimated values, so
the model is refit under two other sets of cut-offs to check the results are not an artefact of them. It is
also scored out of sample: fitted on the first 70% of days and used to classify the last 30%, then compared
with always predicting the most common level.

```{r}
#| output: true

#sensitivity of the odds ratios to the cut-offs: (drop_mod, drop_high, vol_mod, vol_high)
threshold_sets <- list(
  Baseline = c(0.03, 0.07, 1.25, 2),
  Tighter = c(0.02, 0.05, 1.5, 3),
  Wider = c(0.05, 0.10, 1.5, 2.5)
)

sensitivity <- map_dfr(names(threshold_sets), function(nm) {
  th <- threshold_sets[[nm]]
  d <- build_risk_data(th[1], th[2], th[3], th[4])
  m <- MASS::polr(risk_formula, data = d, Hess = TRUE)
  tibble(thresholds = nm, term = names(coef(m)), odds_ratio = as.numeric(exp(coef(m))))
})

sensitivity |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = thresholds, values_from = odds_ratio) |>
  kable(digits = 3) |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 10)

#out-of-sample check: fit on the first 70% of days, classify the last 30%
n_fit <- floor(0.7 * n_risk)
risk_fit_set <- risk_data[1:n_fit, ]
risk_test_set <- risk_data[(n_fit + 1):n_risk, ]

risk_model_oos <- MASS::polr(risk_formula, data = risk_fit_set, Hess = TRUE)
risk_pred <- predict(risk_model_oos, newdata = risk_test_set)

majority_class <- names(which.max(table(risk_fit_set$risk_level)))
actual_level <- as.character(risk_test_set$risk_level)
cat("Out-of-sample accuracy:", round(mean(as.character(risk_pred) == actual_level), 3),
    "| always predicting", majority_class, ":", round(mean(actual_level == majority_class), 3), "\n")
```

# Factor Model
```{}
factor <- MODEL MODEL MODEL
```


# Forecasting/Prediction ML Models

# break up the data

I predict the next day's log return, using the same outcome, the same rows and the same error
measures for every model so the results can be compared directly. The data are split
chronologically into three parts: Train (oldest 60%), Valid (next 20%) and Test (newest 20%). Models
are fitted on Train, and Valid is used to choose their settings (the ridge penalty, the forest's
`mtry` and `nodesize`, and the number of boosting rounds). Each model is then refit on Train and Valid
together and scored once on Test, so Test plays no part in any decision. Next-day returns are very hard
to predict, so every model is shown next to a baseline that always predicts the training average, and a
model only adds value if it beats that baseline.

```{r}
#going to measure price by adjusted close price, so that is my metric of choice
#predicting the next day's log return (in percent) of adjusted close: the predictors come from day t
#and the outcome from day t+1, so no predictor contains the outcome
#log returns are symmetric and far less sensitive to extreme days than simple percent changes
optt_ml <- optt_model_tidy |>
  mutate(
    #outcome: next day's log return, in percent
    next_return = log(lead(Adjusted) / Adjusted) * 100,
    #today's log return, and the 5 days before it (all known at the close of day t)
    return_t0 = log(Adjusted / dplyr::lag(Adjusted, 1)) * 100,
    return_t1 = dplyr::lag(return_t0, 1),
    return_t2 = dplyr::lag(return_t0, 2),
    return_t3 = dplyr::lag(return_t0, 3),
    return_t4 = dplyr::lag(return_t0, 4),
    return_t5 = dplyr::lag(return_t0, 5),
    #volume relative to its own 20 day average (raw volume drifts over 2007-2026)
    #+1 avoids dividing by zero or taking the log of zero on zero volume days
    vol_ratio = log((Volume + 1) / (rollmean(Volume, k = 20, fill = NA, align = "right") + 1))
  ) |>
  #keep only the outcome and the predictors being used. Raw prices are dropped because they are
  #non-stationary, and the date is dropped (below) so trees cannot memorise the time period
  select(Date, next_return, return_t0, return_t1, return_t2, return_t3, return_t4, return_t5,
         rsi, macd_hist, ATR, true_range, vol_ratio) |>
  #drop rows with NA from the lags/rolling windows and the last day (no next day)
  na.omit()

#dates are kept aside for reporting, then dropped so they cannot be used as a predictor
ml_dates <- optt_ml$Date
optt_ml <- optt_ml |> select(-Date)

# split data for training, validation and testing
#60% train, 20% validation, 20% test
#stock data is a time series, so the split is chronological (oldest to Train, newest to Test).
#A random split would train on days that come after the days it is tested on.
n <- nrow(optt_ml)
n_train <- floor(0.6 * n)
n_valid <- floor(0.2 * n)

Train <- optt_ml[1:n_train, ]
Valid <- optt_ml[(n_train + 1):(n_train + n_valid), ]
Test <- optt_ml[(n_train + n_valid + 1):n, ]
TrainValid <- rbind(Train, Valid)

predictors <- setdiff(names(optt_ml), "next_return")
x_train <- as.matrix(Train[, predictors])
x_valid <- as.matrix(Valid[, predictors])
x_test <- as.matrix(Test[, predictors])
y_train <- Train$next_return
y_valid <- Valid$next_return
y_test <- Test$next_return

#one set of error measures used for every model: RMSE, MAE and directional accuracy,
#each next to a baseline that always predicts the training average (direction: always the more common of up / not up)
eval_metrics <- function(actual, pred, train_mean) {
  tibble(
    RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - pred)^2)),
    baseline_RMSE = sqrt(mean((actual - train_mean)^2)),
    MAE = mean(abs(actual - pred)),
    baseline_MAE = mean(abs(actual - train_mean)),
    #direction = up (return above zero) versus not up (zero or down), for the model and the baseline alike
    directional_accuracy = mean((pred > 0) == (actual > 0)),
    baseline_directional = max(mean(actual > 0), mean(actual <= 0))
  )
}

summary(Train)
summary(Valid)
summary(Test)
```

The table below reports the dates covered by each part. The three periods differ in volatility, so
a model's Test error is partly a statement about the period it is tested on.

```{r}
#| output: true

split_summary <- tibble(
  set = c("Train", "Valid", "Test"),
  start = ml_dates[c(1, n_train + 1, n_train + n_valid + 1)],
  end = ml_dates[c(n_train, n_train + n_valid, n)],
  days = c(nrow(Train), nrow(Valid), nrow(Test)),
  mean_return = c(mean(y_train), mean(y_valid), mean(y_test)),
  sd_return = c(sd(y_train), sd(y_valid), sd(y_test)),
  max_abs_return = c(max(abs(y_train)), max(abs(y_valid)), max(abs(y_test)))
)

split_summary |>
  kable(digits = 2) |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 10)
```

Volume has to be on one consistent basis across the whole history for the volume-based variables to mean
the same thing in every period. The table below shows the median and mean daily Volume and the daily return
volatility for each calendar year; a sudden change of orders of magnitude in a single year would point to
a split that has not been adjusted for.

```{r}
#| output: true

optt_model_tidy |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(median_volume = median(Volume),
            mean_volume = mean(Volume),
            return_sd = sd(log(Adjusted / lag(Adjusted)) * 100, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(Year = as.character(Year)) |>
  kable(digits = c(0, 0, 0, 2), format.args = list(big.mark = ",")) |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

## Ridge Regression (results don't mean much now, acts as a stabiliser in the weighted model)

```{r}
# ridge regression on the same Train/Valid/Test split as the other models
#predicting next_return, the same outcome as the random forest and XGBoost
#glmnet standardises the predictors internally, so no scaling is needed here

ridge <- glmnet(x_train, y_train, alpha = 0)

plot(ridge, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE)

#choose lambda on the Valid set (later days than Train, so no look-ahead)
valid_pred_ridge <- predict(ridge, newx = x_valid)
valid_rmse_ridge <- sqrt(colMeans((y_valid - valid_pred_ridge)^2))
best_lambda <- ridge$lambda[which.min(valid_rmse_ridge)]
cat("Best Lambda:", best_lambda, "\n")

#Plot the validation error across lambda
plot(log(ridge$lambda), valid_rmse_ridge, type = "l",
     xlab = "log(lambda)", ylab = "Validation RMSE")
abline(v = log(best_lambda), lty = 2)

#refit on Train + Valid at the chosen lambda, then score Test once
ridge_final <- glmnet(rbind(x_train, x_valid), c(y_train, y_valid), alpha = 0, lambda = best_lambda)

# Extract coefficients at the chosen lambda
final_coefficients <- coef(ridge_final)
print(final_coefficients)

pred_test_ridge <- as.numeric(predict(ridge_final, newx = x_test))
ridge_results <- eval_metrics(y_test, pred_test_ridge, mean(c(y_train, y_valid)))
```

## Random Forest

```{r}
#random forest: choose mtry and nodesize on the Valid set, refit on Train + Valid, then score Test once
set.seed(10092026)
rf_grid <- expand.grid(mtry = c(2, 3, 4, 6, 8), nodesize = c(5, 25, 50))
rf_grid$valid_rmse <- NA_real_

for (g in seq_len(nrow(rf_grid))) {
  fit_g <- randomForest(next_return ~ ., data = Train, ntree = 300,
                        mtry = rf_grid$mtry[g], nodesize = rf_grid$nodesize[g])
  rf_grid$valid_rmse[g] <- sqrt(mean((Valid$next_return - predict(fit_g, Valid))^2))
}

best_rf <- rf_grid[which.min(rf_grid$valid_rmse), ]
print(best_rf)

rf <- randomForest(next_return ~ ., data = TrainValid, ntree = 500, mtry = best_rf$mtry,
                   nodesize = best_rf$nodesize, importance = TRUE)
print(rf)
important <- importance(rf)
print(important)
varImpPlot(rf)

pred_test_rf <- predict(rf, Test)
rf_results <- eval_metrics(y_test, pred_test_rf, mean(TrainValid$next_return))

#can assign weights once I am happy with the model + variables.
#weights <- assign here
#weighted_rf <- randomForest(next_return ~., data = Train, weights = weights)

```

## XGBoost

```{r}
#install.packages("xgboost")
library(xgboost)

dtrain <- xgb.DMatrix(data = x_train, label = y_train)
dvalid <- xgb.DMatrix(data = x_valid, label = y_valid)
dtest  <- xgb.DMatrix(data = x_test, label = y_test)

param <- list(eval_metric = "rmse",
              objective = "reg:squarederror",
              eta = 0.01,
              max_depth = 3,
              subsample = 0.7,
              colsample_bytree = 0.7,
              min_child_weight = 10)

#early stopping watches the LAST entry, so it is the Valid set (Test is never used here)
evals <- list(train = dtrain, valid = dvalid)

set.seed(10092026)
xgb <- xgb.train(params = param,
                 data = dtrain,
                 nrounds = 1000,
                 evals = evals,
                 early_stopping_rounds = 50,
                 print_every_n = 50)

#number of rounds that gave the lowest Valid error
#the log's column is called valid_rmse or valid-rmse depending on the xgboost version, so find it by prefix
eval_log <- as.data.frame(xgb$evaluation_log)
valid_col <- grep("^valid", names(eval_log), value = TRUE)
best_nrounds <- if (length(valid_col) == 1) which.min(eval_log[[valid_col]]) else integer(0)

#fallbacks if this version does not keep the log: the stored best iteration (counted from 0 in the attribute)
if (length(best_nrounds) != 1) best_nrounds <- as.integer(xgb$best_iteration)
if (length(best_nrounds) != 1) {
  best_attr <- xgb.attr(xgb, "best_iteration")
  if (!is.null(best_attr)) best_nrounds <- as.integer(best_attr) + 1
}
stopifnot(length(best_nrounds) == 1, !is.na(best_nrounds)) #stop here, with a clear message, if none of the above worked
cat("XGBoost rounds used for the final fit:", best_nrounds, "\n")

#refit on Train + Valid with that many rounds, then score Test once
dtrainvalid <- xgb.DMatrix(data = rbind(x_train, x_valid), label = c(y_train, y_valid))
set.seed(10092026)
xgb_final <- xgb.train(params = param, data = dtrainvalid, nrounds = best_nrounds, verbose = 0)

pred_test_xgb <- predict(xgb_final, dtest)
xgb_results <- eval_metrics(y_test, pred_test_xgb, mean(c(y_train, y_valid)))
```

## Model Comparison

All three models are scored on the same Test rows with the same outcome. RMSE and MAE are in percentage
points of log return (lower is better), and each is shown next to the baseline that always predicts the
training average. Directional accuracy is the share of days where the model correctly called up (a return above zero)
versus not up (zero or down), next to the share that always predicting the more common of the two would get.

```{r}
#| output: true

model_comparison <- bind_rows(Ridge = ridge_results,
                              `Random Forest` = rf_results,
                              XGBoost = xgb_results,
                              .id = "model")

model_comparison |>
  kable(digits = 3) |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```
